name: Data analyst
summary: Data analyst interviews usually test three things: whether you can get the right numbers out of data (SQL and spreadsheets), whether you can reason about what those numbers mean for the business, and whether you can explain a finding to someone who isn't technical. Many companies add a take-home or live exercise on a small dataset.
rounds: Online test or live exercise: SQL, spreadsheet work and basic statistics
Case or take-home: analyse a small dataset and present what you found (often)
Hiring manager interview on past projects and business sense
looks_for: Accurate SQL: joins, grouping, window functions, handling nulls and duplicates
Turning a vague business question into a metric you can measure
Clear charts and a one-line takeaway

questions.text: Tell me about an analysis you did that changed a decision.
covers: The decision at stake and who was making it
What you analysed and the one finding that mattered
What changed because of it, with a number if you have one

questions.text: Tell me about a time you found a mistake in a report or dataset others were relying on.
covers: How you noticed something was off
How you confirmed it before raising it
How you told people and what you fixed so it didn't recur

questions.text: Describe a time a stakeholder disagreed with what your data showed.
covers: Their view and why it was reasonable to them
How you checked your own numbers again
How you reached a shared answer, or agreed what to test next

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to deliver an analysis with a very tight deadline.
covers: What you cut and what you kept
How you made the limits of a quick answer clear
What you followed up with afterwards

questions.text: Daily orders dropped 15% yesterday. How would you find out why?
covers: Checking the data first: a tracking or pipeline problem, a holiday, a one-off
Breaking the drop down by city, platform, channel and new versus returning users
Stating the most likely cause and how you'd confirm it

questions.text: How would you find the top three products by revenue in each category using SQL? Talk me through it.
covers: Aggregating revenue per product, then ranking within each category
A window function such as ROW_NUMBER or DENSE_RANK, and how ties are treated
Filtering to the top three after ranking, not before

questions.text: What's the difference between an inner join and a left join, and when has the choice mattered in your work?
covers: Inner keeps only matches; left keeps every row of the left table
How a left join shows missing data as nulls and can multiply rows
A real example where the wrong join gave a wrong total

questions.text: How would you measure whether a new checkout design is working?
covers: One main metric (such as checkout conversion) plus guardrails like refunds or support tickets
Comparing fairly: an A/B test, or a before-and-after with care
How long to run it and what result would change the decision

questions.text: Explain a p-value, or statistical significance, to a manager who isn't technical.
covers: A plain-words version: how likely a difference this big is by chance alone
What it doesn't say: how big or important the effect is
An everyday example

questions.text: You're given a messy spreadsheet of customer records. What would you check before analysing it?
covers: Duplicates, missing values, inconsistent formats and impossible values
Where the data came from and what each column really means
Writing down what you cleaned, so others can repeat it

questions.text: Walk me through a dashboard you built. Who used it, and what did you leave out?
covers: Who it was for and the decision it supported
The few metrics on it and why those
What you removed to keep it readable, and how you knew people used it

questions.text: Which tools do you use for analysis, and how do you choose between a spreadsheet, SQL and Python?
covers: Spreadsheets for small, quick or shared work
SQL where the data lives in a database
Python or R for repeatable, larger or statistical work, with an example

questions.text: Why do you want to work as a data analyst?
covers: What you enjoy about the work, shown by something you've done
The kind of business problems you want to work on
Where you want to grow next

questions.text: What do you know about our business, and which metrics would you want to look at first?
covers: How the company makes money, in a sentence
Two or three metrics that follow from that
A question you'd want answered in your first month

tips: Practise writing SQL out loud: say what each step does before you write it.
In a case question, ask what decision the analysis is for before you start.
End every answer with the takeaway in one sentence, then the caveat.
Bring one project you can talk about for ten minutes: the question, the data, the mess, the result.
